Yes—alternative energies can effectively replace fossil fuels, and many places already prove it. Iceland runs on roughly 85% renewables, Paraguay about 99.9%, Costa Rica about 99.78%, and Norway about 98%. That demonstrates renewables are not just theoretical; they can supply huge shares of real electricity demand.

Moreover, to end fossil-fuel dependence quickly, we also need low-carbon nuclear power alongside renewables. Crucially, even in the U.S.—a benchmark for scale and infrastructure—alternative energy use has historically never exceeded about 20%. So the idea that renewables “fill the energy needs of large countries anytime soon” is not realistic; it ignores how hard it is to expand generation and, just as importantly, transmission, storage, and grid reliability fast enough to fully replace fossil fuels.

This is why natural gas should be treated as an appropriate bridge fuel. High-impact accident risk (e.g., Fukushima) undermines the claim that nuclear provides a clean, reliable path without major downsides.

Bottom line: high-renewables examples don’t show that large countries can quickly eliminate fossil fuels, and the U.S. record suggests adoption hasn’t reached the level needed.
